opus-5.5.text:
I think size is one of the most underrated design choices in humanoid robotics. When you make a robot smaller, a lot of things get easier at once. Physics works in your favor: mass scales roughly with the cube of size, while things like muscle or actuator cross-section scale with the square. So a smaller robot is relatively stronger for its weight, it falls with much less energy, and when it falls it usually doesn't break. For research, especially learning-based control, that's huge. You can let the robot try things, fail, get up and try again, without a technician rebuilding a leg every afternoon. It's also cheaper, safer to have around people, and easier to transport and iterate on. In my experience, a small, robust platform lets you collect far more real-world data and run far more experiments per dollar, and right now that iteration speed matters more than anything.

There are real limitations, though. The world is built for human-sized bodies. Counter heights, door handles, shelves, car seats, the tools themselves all assume an adult's reach and strength. A small robot can't load a dishwasher in a normal kitchen or lift a box onto a high shelf without a lot of awkward workarounds. Payload is limited in absolute terms, even if strength-to-weight is good. Some dynamics also don't transfer cleanly. A policy that works on a small, light body won't necessarily carry over to a full-sized one, because inertia, contact forces, and actuator limits all change. So you can't treat the small robot as a perfect proxy for the big one.

So I see it as a question of what you're optimizing for right now. If the goal is to learn fast, to figure out locomotion, manipulation, and whole-body control, to build the data and software stack, then a smaller robot is a great tool, maybe the best one. If the goal is deployment in homes or factories doing real human tasks, eventually you need something close to human scale. My bet is the field benefits from both: small robots as the fast, forgiving research platform where ideas get proven, and full-size robots as the place those ideas finally have to survive contact with the real world.

r001.rationale: It says smaller robots may struggle with human-scale tasks, citing limited reach and difficulty loading a dishwasher or lifting boxes to high shelves.

r002.rationale: It discusses collecting real-world data and transferring policies between robot sizes, but does not raise how human data can be used for smaller humanoid robots.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, this is a question we debate internally almost every week, because size is one of those decisions that touches everything else.

Let me start with why smaller is attractive. The first thing is cost. If you shrink a humanoid from, say, 1.7 meters to something closer to 1.2 or 1.3 meters, your motors can be smaller, your reducers can be smaller, your battery can be smaller. Those three items are most of the bill of materials. The physics works in your favor too, because the torque you need at the joints scales roughly with mass times lever arm, and both of those go down together. So you don't get a linear reduction in cost, you get something better than linear.

The second thing is safety. A smaller, lighter robot simply carries less kinetic energy. If it falls, or if it bumps into a person, the consequences are very different. For anything that is going to operate around families or in a home, I think that matters more than people admit. Nobody wants a 70-kilogram machine losing balance next to their child.

The third thing is iteration speed. A smaller platform is easier to build, easier to repair, easier to ship to a customer or a research lab. When you're still learning what the product even is, that velocity is worth a lot.

Now the limitations, and they are real. The most obvious one is that the human world is built for human dimensions. Counters, door handles, shelves, light switches, the height of a washing machine door. A robot that's too short can't reach a top shelf, can't see over a table, can't lift a box onto a cart at a comfortable height. You can compensate with longer arms or a telescoping torso, but every compensation adds complexity and starts to break the "humanoid" promise, which is that the robot fits into existing environments without modification.

The second limitation is payload. Smaller actuators mean you can carry less. For home tasks that's often fine. For logistics or factory work, where someone wants it to move 15 or 20 kilograms repeatedly, a small robot struggles, and the customer notices immediately.

The third one is subtler. Smaller robots have shorter legs, which means shorter strides and a smaller support polygon, so walking stability and walking speed actually become harder in some ways, not easier. You also have less internal volume for compute, cooling, and batteries, so your runtime per charge can suffer even though the robot is lighter.

So how do I weigh it? I think the honest answer is that there isn't a universally right size, there's a right size for a use case. If I'm targeting a home companion or an education product, I lean smaller, because safety and cost dominate and the tasks are lighter. If I'm targeting industrial work, I lean toward adult human scale, because the environment and the payload are non-negotiable.

What I try to avoid is the trap of picking a size because it demos well. A smaller robot looks cute on stage and it's cheaper to build a fleet of them, but if it can't do the job in the real environment, you've just made a very good toy. And conversely, a full-size robot looks impressive, but if it's too heavy and too expensive to ever deploy in a home, you've built a very good research platform. The discipline is to start from the task and the environment, and let that pull the size, rather than the other way around.

r001.rationale: It explains that smaller robots may not reach shelves or handles and may struggle with tasks requiring greater reach or lifting, reducing their ability to perform tasks in human environments.

astra-6.text:
I’d start with what you want the robot to do. Making a humanoid smaller can reduce material costs, make it easier to transport and test, and lower the potential impact of a collision. That can be useful for research or for tasks in confined spaces.

But you also give up reach, payload, and room for batteries and actuators. A smaller robot may struggle with stairs, doors, or countertops designed for people. And miniaturization doesn’t automatically make engineering easier—you still need to fit sensing, computing, cooling, and wiring into a tighter space.

So I wouldn’t say smaller is inherently better. If the goal is a platform for learning and experimentation, there are strong advantages. If the goal is to do useful physical work in a human environment, the right size comes from the task: what it needs to reach, what it needs to carry, and how long it needs to operate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the right size depends on what you want the robot to do. Making a humanoid smaller can reduce material costs, make it easier to transport, and make testing safer because there’s less mass involved. That can be very useful for research and for getting more people access to the hardware.

But smaller doesn’t automatically mean easier. You have less space for batteries, motors, computing, and cooling. And if the robot is meant to work in a human environment, size matters: can it reach a countertop, open a door, or carry the things you need it to carry? A small robot may demonstrate a skill beautifully without being able to perform the same job in a real setting.

So I’d start with the task and work backward. The goal is to make it as small as you can while still meeting the requirements for reach, strength, runtime, and reliability.
